metadata.title: Targeting VEGF signaling and stromal remodeling enhances chemoimmunotherapy efficacy in esophageal cancer

sections.text: Abstract Background Neoadjuvant chemoimmunotherapy (NACI) has shown promising results in treating esophageal squamous cell carcinoma (ESCC), yet the mechanisms driving its efficacy remain poorly defined, limiting further optimization of this regimen. Methods To investigate the dynamics of the tumor microenvironment (TME), we integrated single-cell RNA sequencing, immunorepertoire profiling, and spatial transcriptomics across 18 samples from nine patients with ESCC undergoing NACI. Computational workflows encompassed integrated clustering, gene set enrichment, T cell receptor repertoire characterization, copy number variation estimation, and cell–cell communication inference. Spatial mapping was performed using cytoSPACE. Key findings were validated via orthogonal spatial transcriptomics, multiplex immunohistochemistry, and in vivo preclinical models. Results We identified distinct post-treatment accumulation of ACKR1+ endothelial cells (ECs) and CFD+ cancer-associated fibroblasts (CAFs) at tumor boundaries, potentially correlating with enhanced CD8+ T cell infiltration and improved clinical outcomes. Conversely, treatment-resistant tumors exhibited VEGFA-driven upregulation in malignant cells, promoting RGCC+ ECs with elevated VEGFR2 expression. These RGCC+ ECs synergized with MMP11+ CAFs to form a collagen-rich tumor niche that fostered malignancy and immunosuppression. Importantly, targeting VEGFR2 not only improved therapeutic response but also reversed immune suppression. Conclusions This study reveals that stromal cells such as CAFs and ECs within the TME collaboratively determine NACI efficacy in ESCC. These findings could offer novel theoretical insights and actionable strategies for enhancing treatment efficacy in ESCC.

In recent years, immune checkpoint inhibitors have emerged as a transformative approach in cancer therapy by reshaping the tumor microenvironment (TME), 1 2 leading to improved clinical outcomes across various malignancies. In particular, programmed cell death protein-1 (PD-1) inhibitors have demonstrated significant survival benefits when used as first-line treatment for advanced esophageal squamous cell carcinoma (ESCC). 3 Moreover, the integration of neoadjuvant chemoimmunotherapy (NACI) into the management of locally advanced ESCC has shown promise in increasing the probability of R0 resection and pathological complete response (pCR), 4 5 offering a potentially curative option for a subset of patients. Despite these advances, several critical challenges remain in the effective application of chemoimmunotherapy (NACI) for ESCC. First, a substantial proportion of patients exhibit either primary or acquired resistance to treatment, limiting its broader efficacy. Second, pCR rates among patients undergoing surgery after NACI exceed 30%, but there remains an urgent need to further enhance therapeutic outcomes. 6 To achieve this, a deeper understanding of the mechanisms underlying response and resistance to NACI is essential for guiding the development of next-generation treatment strategies. Although programmed death-ligand 1 (PD-L1) expression has been widely studied as a potential biomarker for immunotherapy response across multiple cancers, its predictive value in ESCC remains controversial. 7 8 For instance, findings from the KEYNOTE-590 trial indicated that patients with PD-L1 Combined Positive Score ≥10 experienced significantly prolonged survival when treated with pembrolizumab plus chemotherapy. 9 In contrast, the ESCORT trial failed to demonstrate a clear correlation between PD-L1 expression and clinical benefit, 10 suggesting that the mechanisms governing response to chemoimmunotherapy combinations may differ fundamentally from those of monotherapy. These discrepancies highlight the pressing need for more accurate and clinically relevant biomarkers to guide patient selection and treatment decisions. Emerging evidence from bulk RNA sequencing and multiplex immunohistochemistry (mIHC) studies underscores the pivotal role of the TME in determining the efficacy of immunotherapy. 11 13 Various cellular components—including tumor-infiltrating lymphocytes, fibroblasts and myeloid-derived suppressor cells—have been implicated in modulating antitumor immunity. However, such bulk analysis methods inherently obscure the heterogeneity of individual cell populations and their functional states. In contrast, single-cell sequencing and spatial transcriptomics (ST) offer unprecedented resolution by dissecting the complex cellular composition and interactions within the TME at the cellular level. 14 15 These technologies have already provided valuable insights in cancers such as liver cancer, glioblastoma and lung cancer, informing novel diagnostic and therapeutic strategies. 16 18 To date, most single-cell studies in ESCC have focused on untreated tumors, 19 20 leaving a critical gap in understanding of how the TME evolves during NACI. Recent investigations employing single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq) and T cell receptor (TCR) profiling of tumor and peripheral blood samples from patients with ESCC before and after treatment have begun to shed light on immune dynamics associated with therapeutic response. These studies identified several immune subsets linked to treatment response, including SPRY1+CD8+ exhausted T cell (Tex) cells, CXCL13+CD8+ Tex cells, regulatory T cells (Tregs), TRGC2+ natural killer T (NKT) cells, and tertiary lymphoid structures (TLSs). Poor responders show enrichment of terminally exhausted CD8+ Tex cells and CD4+ Treg-TNFRSF4 cells, while better outcomes correlate with progenitor-like SPRY1+CD8+ Tex cells associated with TLS and M1-like macrophages. 21 22 LRRC15+ cancer-associated fibroblasts (CAFs) and SPP1+ macrophages contribute to immunosuppression by recruiting Tregs. TRGC2+ NKT cells are recruited to tumors via chemokines like CCL5 and CCL21, potentially enhancing therapeutic efficacy. 23 Overall, chemoimmunotherapy partially reshapes the TME by modulating T cell infiltration, but interactions involving other stromal components remain poorly understood, highlighting the need for further investigation into the broader TME landscape in ESCC. One major limitation of conventional scRNA-seq lies in the loss of spatial context, which hinders the ability to study cellular localization, tissue architecture, and intercellular communication. ST addresses this issue by preserving the spatial organization of gene expression within the tissue. Several studies applying this technology have revealed spatially coordinated interactions—for example, between distinct CAF subtypes and macrophage populations—that contribute to the formation of immunosuppressive niches. 15 24 25 In ESCC, ST analyses have uncovered dynamic crosstalk between CAFs and tumor cells during malignant progression, implicating these interactions in immune evasion, extracellular matrix remodeling, and invasive tumor margin formation. 26 Despite these insights, few studies have applied ST to investigate NACI response in ESCC, underscoring the urgency of expanding this line of research. In this study, we employed an integrative approach combining scRNA-seq, TCR sequencing (scTCR-seq), and ST to comprehensively profile tumor samples from patients with ESCC before and after NACI. By capturing both cellular heterogeneity and spatial organization, we aimed to dissect the multicellular dynamics within the TME, focusing on the interactions among malignant epithelial cells, stromal cells, and immune compartments. Our goal was to uncover the molecular and cellular mechanisms driving differential responses to treatment and to identify novel therapeutic vulnerabilities that could be exploited to improve clinical outcomes. Through this multidimensional analysis, we sought to provide a detailed mechanistic framework for future precision NACI strategies in ESCC.

Nine patients pathologically diagnosed with ESCC were included in the single-cell sequencing study. The patient had not received tumor-related immunotherapy, chemotherapy, or radiation therapy before the first endoscopic sampling. The patient was then treated with NACI consisting of 200 mg of carelizumab, carboplatin (area under the curve=5) and 260 mg/m 2 albumin-bound paclitaxel every 3 weeks. After two cycles of treatment, tumor tissues were sampled again by either surgery resection or endoscopic sampling if surgery was not planned. A total of 18 samples before or after NACI were sent for single-cell sequencing. Four ESCC paraffin samples were used for ST. Among them, one is surgery without other treatment, and three were surgical samples after NACI. Immunohistochemistry (IHC) and mIHC were performed on 14 pre-NACI or post-NACI paraffin samples. Clinical efficacy was assessed on the basis of Response Evaluation Criteria in Solid Tumors (RECIST) V.1.1. Clinical information of the tumor samples is summarized in online supplemental table S1 .

The tissue samples were processed as described below. Briefly, samples were first washed with phosphate-buffered saline (PBS), minced into small pieces (≈1 mm 3 ) on ice and enzymatically digested with Human tumor Dissociation kit (Miltenyi Biotech) and 1 mg/mL Dispase II (Sigma) for 35 min at 37℃, with agitation. After digestion, samples were sieved through a 70 µm cell strainer, and centrifuged at 400× g for 5 min. After washing with PBS containing 0.04% BSA (Bovine Serum Albumin), the cell pellets were re-suspended in PBS containing 0.04% BSA and refiltered through a 35 µm cell strainer. Dissociated single cells were then stained with acridine orange (AO)/propidium iodide (PI) for viability assessment using Countstar Fluorescence Cell Analyzer.

The scRNA-Seq libraries and V(D)J libraries were generated using the 10X Genomics Chromium Controller Instrument and Chromium Single Cell 5’ library and gel bead kit, along with the V(D)J enrichment kit (10X Genomics, Pleasanton, California, USA). Briefly, cells were concentrated to approximately 1,000 cells/µL and loaded into each channel to generate single-cell Gel Bead-In-Emulsions (GEMs). After the Reverse Transcription (RT) step, GEMs were broken and barcoded-complementary DNA (cDNA) was purified and amplified. The amplified barcoded cDNA was used to construct 5’ gene expression libraries and TCR enriched libraries. For 5’ library construction, the amplified barcoded cDNA was fragmented, A-tailed, ligated with adaptors and index PCR amplified. For the V(D)J library, human T cell V(D)J sequences were enriched from the amplified cDNA followed by fragmentation, A-tailing, adaptor ligation and index PCR amplification. The final libraries were quantified using the Qubit High Sensitivity DNA assay (Thermo Fisher Scientific) and the size distribution of the libraries was determined using a High Sensitivity DNA chip on a Bioanalyzer 2200 (Agilent). All libraries were sequenced by Illumina sequencer (Illumina, San Diego, California, USA) on a 150 bp paired-end run.

Quality control and adapter trimming of the raw FASTQ files were performed using fastp (V.0.21.0) with default parameters. 27 Gene expression matrices for each sample were generated by aligning reads to the human reference genome (GRCh38 Ensemble: V.104) using CellRanger (V.3.1.0). The resulting count matrices were analyzed using the Seurat package (V.4.3.0) within the R environment (V.4.2.2). 28 Low-quality cells were excluded based on the criteria of expressing fewer than 200 genes and having a mitochondrial unique molecular identifier (UMI) fraction greater than 20%. Potential doublets for individual samples were detected and removed using the DoubletFinder package (V.2.0.3). 29 Following filtering, the objects for each sample were merged. The combined gene expression matrix was normalized using the NormalizeData function. Subsequently, the normalized data were scaled and centered with the ScaleData function, regressing out the variable ‘nCount_RNA’. Principal component analysis (PCA) was conducted using the RunPCA function on the scaled data, based on the top 2,000 highly variable genes (HVGs) identified via the FindVariableFeatures function employing the vst method. The first 15 principal components were then used to construct a shared nearest neighbor (SNN) graph by identifying each cell’s 200 nearest neighbors with the FindNeighbors function. Cells were clustered using the Louvain algorithm implemented in the FindClusters function, with a resolution parameter set to 0.4. Finally, dimensionality reduction was performed using the RunUMAP function, applying the ‘umap-learn’ method. During cell cluster annotation, differentially expressed genes (DEGs) for each cluster were identified using the Wilcoxon rank-sum test, with criteria of |log₂ fold change|≥0.25, adjusted p value <0.05, detection fraction exceeding 0.1 in either of the two groups, and a difference in detection fraction between groups greater than 0.1. Clusters were then classified and annotated based on the expression of validated canonical markers representing specific cell types. Major cell lineages were assigned as follows: epithelial cells ( EPCAM, KRT8 ), fibroblasts ( LUM, COL1A1, DCN ), endothelial cells (ECs) ( PECAM1, VWF ), NK-T cells ( CD3D, CD3E, CD3G ), B cells ( CD79A, CD19, MS4A1 ), plasma cells ( CD79A, JCHAIN, MS4A1 ), myeloid cells ( CD14, LYZ, CSF1R ), neutrophils ( CSF3R, G0S1 ), and mast cells ( CPA3, KIT ).

Each major cell population was extracted for subclustering as described above. After the initial subclustering, we observed batch effects and detected some cells expressing multiple lineage markers, likely doublets missed by DoubletFinder. These doublets were manually removed before performing the second clustering. To further correct batch effects, Harmony (V.1.2.3) was applied with default settings. 30 Epithelial cells, ECs, fibroblasts, myeloid cells, and B cells/plasma cells were then clustered separately at resolutions of 2.0, 0.4, 1.6, 1.4, and 1.0, respectively. Due to overlapping gene expression profiles between certain T and NK cell populations, clustering alone was insufficient to distinguish them reliably. To enhance T cell identification, potential T cells were first isolated using two criteria: (1) expression of T cell markers ( CD3D, CD3E, CD3G ), and (2) presence of rearranged αβ TCR genes. These candidate T cells were subsequently mapped to a well-annotated cellular indexing of transcriptomes and epitopes by sequencing (CITE-seq) reference dataset, comprising 162,000 peripheral blood mononuclear cells labeled with 228 antibodies and annotated with predefined CD4, CD8, and “Other T” cell subsets. 31 To align our data with the reference, the T cell expression matrix was normalized using SCTransform. 32 Anchors between the datasets were identified through Seurat’s FindTransferAnchors function with default parameters, leveraging the reference’s precomputed supervised PCA. Cell type annotations and protein expression profiles were then transferred to our T cells using MapQuery, thereby enabling accurate classification into CD4, CD8, and other T cell subtypes. 33 Ultimately, 11,426 CD8 T cells and 10,040 CD4 T cells were annotated. Subsequent clustering and annotation analyses of these subsets were conducted at resolutions of 1.6 and 1.2 for CD8 and CD4 T cells, respectively.

TCR sequencing data were processed using the “cellranger vdj” function within the Cell Ranger toolkit (V.7.1.0), aligned to the human GRCh38 reference genome (10 Genomics). After assembly, rigorous quality control retained only high-confidence TCR sequences with full-length coverage, valid cell barcodes, and unambiguous chain assignments. Potential doublets were excluded by removing cells with more than two pairs of chains. After quality filtering, only cells meeting one of the following criteria were retained: T cell with no TCR chains detected, a single T cell receptor β (TRB) chain, a paired T cell receptor α (TRA) and TRB chain, or one TRB chain with two TRA chains. 34 TCR diversity reflects the breadth and evenness of the TCR repertoire, encompassing both the number of unique clonotypes (richness) and the uniformity of their frequency distribution (evenness). Diversity was quantified using Shannon entropy, calculated via the vegan R package (V.2.6.10), 35 with the formula: Where denotes the relative frequency of clonotype , and is the total number of unique clonotypes in the sample. TCR clonality measures the extent to which the repertoire is dominated by highly expanded clones. It was computed based on the frequencies of all productive TCR sequences, following a previously described method. 36 Here, represents the frequency of clone in a sample with unique clones. The clonality metric was normalized by the total number of unique clones, yielding values between 0 and 1. Higher values indicate a repertoire skewed toward dominant, expanded clones. Intergroup differences were evaluated using paired two-sided Wilcoxon tests. Expanded clonotypes were defined as those detected in at least two cells. To determine which CD8+ T cell subtypes exhibited significant TCR expansion for a given patient following treatment, we employed a beta-binomial model that accounts for variance from random sampling and incorporates time-dependent variance arising from the highly diverse repertoire. 37 We then calculated the proportion of CD8+ T cells subpopulations with significantly expanded (Ex) and non-significantly expanded (nEx) TCRs separately within responder and non-responder groups. Statistical significance was assessed using the χ² test between Ex and nEx CD8+ T cells, followed by Benjamini-Hochberg correction to adjust the p values. To further characterize the molecular features of CD8+T cell subtypes displaying significant TCR expansion, differential gene expression analysis was conducted using Seurat’s FindMarkers function with default parameters, comparing the Ex CD8+ T cells to the non-naïve nEx (ex) CD8+T cells. Genes with a log fold change greater than 0.5 and an adjusted p value below 0.01 were deemed differentially expressed. Shared clonotypes were operationally defined as TCRs detected in at least one cell in two or more distinct cellular clusters. To assess whether the overlap of clonotypes between distinct cell clusters differed before and after treatment in responder and non-responder samples, we first quantified the number of shared clonotypes between clusters across the time point of treatment. Subsequently, a one-sided Fisher’s exact test was performed to evaluate the statistical significance of clonotype overlap between clusters, with p values adjusted for multiple testing using the Benjamini-Hochberg procedure. 33

To infer developmental trajectories and dynamic state transitions within the CD8+ T cell populations, we performed pseudotime analysis using diffusion maps. 38 The pre-processed Seurat object was converted into a SingleCellExperiment format. We then extracted the first 20 dimensions of the Harmony batch-corrected embeddings and used this matrix as input to the DiffusionMap function in the destiny (V.3.24.0) R package. 39 This approach allowed us to calculate diffusion components and computationally order cells along their inferred developmental axes.

sections.section: Cnv Estimation And Malignant Epithelial Cell Identification
sections.text: To identify malignant epithelial cells, we used the inferCNV (V.1.23.0) to evaluate the copy number variations (CNVs) of each epithelial cell. 40 We randomly selected 1,000 ECs and 1,000 fibroblasts as reference normal cells and extracted 500 ECs and 500 fibroblasts as spike-in cells. All epithelial cells, together with these spike-in cells, were designated as the predictor group. Hierarchical clustering using the “ward_D2” method was performed, and tumor cells were clustered according to the clustering information derived from the epithelial cells. The analysis was conducted in “subcluster” mode with denoising applied to improve data quality. We calculated the CNV score for epithelial cells in each hierarchical cluster. The inferCNV output was first normalized by subtracting one to set the baseline to zero. The mean squared CNV value across all genes was computed for each cell as the CNV score. CNV scores of clusters were then compared with the spike-in reference group. Cluster 3 clustered with the reference and showed similar CNV scores, thus was classified as normal epithelial cells; all other clusters were deemed malignant. Additionally, normal epithelial cells exhibited lower signature scores of ESCC malignant-related genes ( EPCAM, TSTA3, NECTIN4, SFN, KRT13, KRT16, KRT17, KRT18, KRT6A, KRT6B ) compared with malignant cells. 41

To identify molecular differences between ACKR1+ and RGCC+ endothelial cells (ECs), we performed differential expression analysis using the FindMarkers function with the Wilcoxon test. DEGs were selected based on |log2(fold change)| > 0, adjusted p value <0.05, and a difference in expression proportion >0.1 between the two cell populations. The same approach was applied to compare malignant epithelial cells between responder and non-responder groups before and after treatment. Differential genes were identified using criteria of |log2(fold change)| > 0.25, adjusted p value <0.01, and an expression proportion fold change >1.5. Based on these DEGs, we conducted pathway enrichment analysis for Gene Ontology (GO) focusing on biological processes using clusterProfiler (V.4.6.2). 42

To characterize the molecular functions of ACKR1+ and RGCC+ ECs, we performed gene set enrichment analysis (GSEA) using fgsea (V.1.24.0) with the MSigDB database, which includes GO and Kyoto Encyclopedia of Genes and Genomes pathways. 43 44 AUCell (V.1.20.2) was employed to assess cellular phenotypes and biological processes, including signatures of CAFs, M1/M2 macrophages, CD8+ T cells with significantly expanded TCR clonotypes (CD8T_Ex), and established gene sets involving immune effector functions, differentiation state, angiogenesis, collagen metabolism, and major histocompatibility complex (MHC)-I activity. 3345 49 Those genes are listed in online supplemental table S4 . Pathway activity scores for angiogenesis-related and vasculogenesis-related GO terms were quantified in malignant epithelial cells across different treatment groups using irGSEA (V.3.3.2) in the R environment (V.4.3.3), integrating four scoring methods (AUCell, UCell, ssGSEA, and SingleScore). 50

CellChat (V.2.1.2) was employed to infer the ligand–receptor interactions between cell types for the pre-R, pre-NR, post-R, and post-NR. 51 The CellChat objects were created based on the normalized expression data and relevant metadata labels. The communication probabilities were inferred using the computeCommunProb function with the default parameters after identifying the overexpressed genes and interactions. Subsequently, communication probability at the signaling pathway level was calculated using the computeCommunProbPathway function. To investigate significant interactions among key cell types between non-responders and responders before and after treatment, the CellChat objects for PRE-NR and PRE-R, as well as POST-R and POST-NR, were merged. Increased ligand-receptor signaling pairs in PRE-NR or POST-R compared with PRE-R or POST-NR were identified using the netVisual_bubble function.

sections.section: Preprocessing And Clustering Of Spatial Transcriptome
sections.text: ST data from four slices—treatment naive (PRE), stable disease (SD), partial response (PR), and complete response (CR)—were processed using SpaceRanger (V.3.0.0) to align raw sequencing reads to the human reference genome, generating expression matrices and spatial coordinates for each slice. Spots expressing fewer than 50 genes were excluded. Each count matrix was normalized with SCTransform, regressing out total counts per spot (vars.to.regress), and 2,000 HVGs were identified per slice using the vst method. The four datasets were then merged. After merging the HVGs from the four slices, a total of 7306 unique genes were used for PCA. Batch effects were corrected using Harmony. An SNN graph was constructed based on the first 20 principal components, considering 150 nearest neighbors per spot via Seurat’s FindNeighbors. Clustering was performed using the Louvain algorithm at a resolution of 1.8 to define major spatial domains by Seurat’s FindClusters. Clusters were visualized with uniform manifold approximation and projection (UMAP) using the umap-learn method and a min.dist of 1.5 with the RunUMAP function. Cluster marker genes were identified using the Wilcoxon rank-sum test by Seurat’s FindAllMarkers with log2(fold change) > 0.25, min.pct>0.1, and adjusted p value <0.05. To visualize the spatial distribution of cell types identified through single-cell analysis, we computed enrichment scores for the top 15 DEGs in each population using ST data with AUCell. Cell type-specific gene signatures were extracted for major populations and subpopulations, including ACKR1+ and RGCC+ ECs, SFRP4+, MMP11+, APOD+, and CFD+ CAFs, CXCL13+ and RGS1+CD8+ T cells, and CD1C+ conventional dendritic cell type 2 (cDC2).

sections.section: Definition Of The Boundary Around The Tumor
sections.text: Based on pathological features of tissue sections, tumor regions and adjacent normal areas were delineated. To better characterize changes in tissue composition within the TME, we defined the tumor boundary region according to the spatial distribution of major cell types identified from single-cell data. First, the top 10 cell-type-specific DEGs were selected by ranking according to log2(fold change) and differences in expression proportion between groups, serving as signatures. Using AUCell, enrichment scores of these cell-type-specific gene sets were calculated in the STs data. Then, the tumor region was defined as the region of interest, and the RadialDistance function in the semla (V.1.1.6) tool was used to compute distances from the border of the tumor. 52 Based on these distances, we analyzed the variation of enrichment activity of cell type-specific gene sets along the distance gradient. Notably, within a 500 µm zone of adjacent normal tissue from the border of the tumor, significant changes in enrichment activity were observed across multiple cell types, thereby defining this zone as the tumor boundary region.

To characterize the spatial distribution of cell types within the TME, we employed cytoSPACE (V.1.0.6a0) to map single-cell data with detailed subpopulation annotations onto ST data, assuming an average of five cells per spot for the 10x Visium data. 53 cytoSPACE assigns single cells to spatial locations by minimizing a correlation-based cost function via a shortest augmenting path optimization routine. For PR and CR samples, single-cell transcriptomic references from the same patients were used for mapping. In the absence of matched data for SD samples, single-cell transcriptomes from non-responders P05, P07, and P09 after treatment were used. The input files required for cytoSPACE were generated from Seurat objects of single-cell and ST data via the R script generate_cytospace_from_seurat_object.R.

To evaluate spatial colocalization of cell types within local neighborhoods, we conducted a colocalization analysis using mapped single-cell data integrated with spatial coordinates derived from ST. Initially, Euclidean distances between mapped cells were computed, defining pairs within a distance of three units as colocalized. For each cell type, the proportion of neighboring cells of other cell types within this region was quantified. To identify statistically significant colocalization patterns, we implemented a permutation test. The spatial positions of mapped cells were randomly permuted, and colocalization proportions within the specified radius were recalculated. This procedure was iterated 1,000 times to establish a null distribution. The observed colocalization proportions were then contrasted with the null distribution, and cell type pairs yielding a p value below 0.05 were deemed to display significant spatial colocalization. The significance was indicated by -log10(p value).

To systematically characterize the spatial co-expression patterns of VEGFA and VEGFR2 (KDR) in ST data, we employed the following analytical framework. First, a Gaussian mixture model (GMM) was applied to stratify individual spots based on VEGFA and KDR expression levels. Spots were classified as “High” if exceeding the mean expression level, otherwise “Low”. Based on these classifications, spots with high expression of both VEGFA and KDR were defined as “VEGFA-KDR”, those with only VEGFA high expression as “VEGFA”, those with only KDR high expression as “KDR”, and all others as “Other”. Second, given the paracrine nature of VEGF signaling with a maximum effective diffusion distance of 200 µm, we implemented a quantitative neighborhood assessment. We randomly sampled 50 tumor-region spots per section (excluding spots with incomplete two-ring neighborhoods within a 200 µm radius). The cumulative count of VEGFA-KDR adjacent co-expression within each sampled spot’s 200 µm neighborhood was calculated. This spatial sampling protocol was repeated 500 times to ensure statistical robustness. Finally, the statistical significance of differences in VEGFA-KDR adjacent coexpression among response groups was assessed using a t-test.

Dewaxing and hydration: The paraffin sections were immersed in sequence in environmentally friendly dewaxing transparent liquid I for 20 min, environmentally friendly dewaxing transparent liquid II for 20 min, anhydrous ethanol I for 5 min, anhydrous ethanol II for 5 min, 75% ethyl alcohol for 5 min, and then rinsed with tap water. Hematoxylin staining: Put sections into hematoxylin solution for 3–5 min, rinse with tap water. Then treat the section with hematoxylin differentiation solution, rinse with tap water. Treat the section with hematoxylin bluing solution, rinse with tap water. Eosin staining: Place the sections in sequence in 95% ethanol for 1 min, eosin dye for 15 s. Dehydration and sealing: Put the sections into absolute ethanol I for 5 min, absolute ethanol II for 5 min, absolute ethanol III for 5 min, xylene I for 5 min, xylene II for 5 min, sealing with neutral gum. Finally, microscopic examination and image acquisition were performed.

Paraffin sections dewaxing to water: Put the sections into environmentally friendly dewaxing solution I for 10 min, environmentally friendly dewaxing solution II for 10 min, environmentally friendly dewaxing solution III for 10 min, anhydrous ethanol I for 5 min, anhydrous ethanol II for 5 min, anhydrous ethanol III for 5 min, distilled water in turn. Antigen repair: EDTA (PH 9.0) was used in a microwave oven for 10 min on medium fire, 5 min off fire, 5 min on low fire, 2 min off fire, and 5 min on low fire. After natural cooling, the slide was placed in PBS (PH 7.4) and washed by shaking on the decolorizing shaker three times, 5 min each time. Blocking endogenous peroxidase: The slices were placed in 3% hydrogen peroxide solution, incubated at room temperature away from light for 25 min, and the slides were placed in PBS (PH 7.4) and washed three times on a decolorizing shaking table for 5 min each time. Serum closure: The tissue was uniformly covered with 3% BSA in the tissue chemical circle and closed at room temperature for 30 min. (Primary antibody of goat origin is blocked with rabbit serum, other sources are blocked with BSA). Add primary antibody: Gently shake off the sealing solution, add PBS to the section in a certain proportion of primary antibody CD3 (Servicebio) or von Willebrand Factor (VWF) (Servicebio), and the section is placed flat in a wet box at 4°C for overnight incubation. Adding secondary antibody: The slide was placed in PBS (PH 7.4) and washed by shaking on the decolorizing shaker three times, 5 min each time. After the slices were slightly dried, the tissue was covered with the secondary antibody labeled with horseradish peroxidase (HRP) of the corresponding species of the primary antibody, and incubated at room temperature for 50 min. Diaminobenzidine (DAB) color development: The slide was placed in PBS (PH 7.4) and washed by shaking on the decolorizing table three times, 5 min each time. After the sections were slightly dried, the freshly prepared DAB color developing solution was added into the circle. The color developing time was controlled under the microscope. The positive color was brown and yellow, and the sections were rinsed with tap water to terminate the color development. Restaining nuclei: hematoxylin restaining for about 3 min, washing with tap water, hematoxylin differentiation solution for a few seconds, rinsing with tap water, hematoxylin returned to blue solution, and rinse with rinsing water. Dewatering and sealing: Put the slices into 75% alcohol for 5 min, 85% alcohol for 5 min, anhydrous ethanol for 5 min, anhydrous ethanol for 5 min, n-butanol for 5 min, xylene for 5 min to dehydrate and transparent, take the slices out of xylene to dry slightly, and seal the slices with glue. Microscopy: The results are interpreted under a white light microscope.

Multiplex immunohistochemistry (mIHC) staining was performed using a four-color multifluorescent immunohistochemical staining kit (Absin). mIHC was performed according to the manufacturer’s protocol. Deparaffinized and hydrated: the sections were covered with xylene three times for 10 min; The sections were covered with 100%, 95%, and 70% ethanol for 5, 5, and 2 min, respectively. The slices were washed three times for 1 min. The plates were covered with 10% formalin for 10 min, then rinsed with water for 1 min, and repeated three times. Microwave antigen repair: the sections were immersed in antigen repair solution, then boiled in microwave oven on high heat and maintained on low heat for 15 min. The blocking solution was added by dropping, and the mixture was humidified and shaken for 10 min at room temperature. Primary antibody incubation: diluted primary antibody solution was added dropwise, shaken and humidified at room temperature for 1 hour, and then the sections were washed with Tris-buffered saline with Tween 20 (TBST) for 3 min. Secondary antibody incubation: HRP secondary antibody working solution was dropped, incubated at room temperature and moistened for 10 min, and then the sections were washed with TBST for 3 min. Amplification signal of fluorescent staining: 100 µL of dye working solution was dropped, and incubated for 10 min at room temperature with moistening and shaking. The slices were washed three times with TBST for 3 min. After microwave repair, sections were washed once with water and covered with TBST for 2 min. For nuclear staining and sealing, 1× 4′,6‑diamidino‑2‑phenylindole (DAPI) working solution was dropped and incubated at room temperature for 5 min. The slices were washed three times with TBST for 2 min. The slides were then sealed with a cover glass. The final results were observed and analyzed by fluorescence microscopy.

ESCC cell lines (KYSE70) (RRID: CVCL_1356) were obtained from Anwei-sci Cell Center, Shanghai, China (Cell NO.AW-CH1203). It was cultured in RMPI 1640 medium (Gibco) supplemented with 10% fetal bovine serum (FBS) (VivaCell) and 1% penicillin–streptomycin (Gibco). KYSE-30 (RRID: CVCL_1351) cell line was obtained from Pricella, Wuhan, China (Cell NO.CL-0577). It was cultured in RMPI 1640 medium (Gibco), Ham’s F-12 (Gibco), 2 mM L-Glutamine (Pricella), 10% FBS (VivaCell) and 1% penicillin–streptomycin. The mouse ESCC cell line AKR was purchased from Shanghai BinSui Biological Technology. The AKR cell line is a widely used syngeneic model that harbors a relatively low tumor mutational burden (TMB) compared with other common murine ESCC cell lines. Consequently, this model exhibits a moderate response to anti-PD-1 monotherapy, which is considerably less robust than that observed in high-TMB ESCC models. 54 57 It was cultured in Dulbecco’s Modified Eagle’s Medium (Gibco) supplemented with 10% FBS (VivaCell) and 1% penicillin–streptomycin. All were maintained in a humidified chamber with 5% CO2 at 37℃. Apatinib, abraxane and DDP were used in the present in vitro studies. The stock solution containing apatinib (Hengrui Pharmaceutical Company), abraxane (Shijiazhuang Pharmaceutical Company) and DDP (Selleck) was prepared in dimethyl sulfoxide (DMSO).

KYSE30 and KYSE70 cells were maintained in 96-well plates (5,000 cells/well) and treated with 0, 10, 20, 30, 40 and 80 µmol/L apatinib. Cell viability was determined by CCK-8 assay after 24 and 48 hours. Then, the experiment is divided into eight groups: control group (DMSO), Apatinib group, CDDP group, Abraxane group, Apatinib+CDDP group, Apatinib+Abraxane group, CDDP+Abraxane group, and Apatinib+CDDP+Abraxane group. ESCC cells (KYSE30 and KYSE70) were maintained in 96-well plates (5,000 cells/well) and treated with agents. After 48 hours, cell viability was determined by CCK-8 assay.

Cell apoptosis was detected by Annexin V-APC/PI apoptosis detection kit (Elabscience). Cells were seeded in 24-well plates and treated with drugs. The treated cells (KYSE30 and KYSE70) were collected and washed twice with cold PBS. The cells were centrifuged at 300 g for 5 min and resuspended at a density of 1×10 6 /mL. The cells were stained with Annexin V and PI in the dark, and the data were analyzed by flow cytometry.

C57BL/6J mice (male, 4–6 weeks old) were purchased from Zhuhai Bestest Bio-Tech. The mice were randomly separated into designated groups by an independent person. No spontaneous regression occurred after subcutaneous injection of 3×10 6 AKR cells per site. After 10 days, the subcutaneous tumor exceeded 200 mm 3 and treatment was started. For antibody-based drug intervention, anti-PD-1 antibody (5 mg/kg; BioXCell), anti-VEFGR2 antibody (10 mg/kg; BioXCell) or immunoglobulin G (control; BioXCell) was injected intraperitoneally every 3 days. Mouse weight and subcutaneous tumor volume were measured every 3 days. The tumor volume was calculated using the formula (length×width 2 )/2. At the end point of the experiment, the mice were killed using cervical dislocation. The tumors were excised for subsequent analysis. The animal study was carried out in accordance with approved protocol.

Tumor tissues were washed twice with 0.9% saline. The tumor tissue was cut to 1 mm 3 and digested with 0.5 mg/mL collagenase IV and 0.1 mg/mL Dnase I for 30 min in a 37°C incubator. The tissue was then passed through a 40 µm cell strainer. ACK Lysis Buffer (LEAGENE) was added to the filtrate, mixed upside down and allowed to stand for 5 min, followed by centrifugation at 300 g for 5 min. The cells were washed twice with PBS solution containing 2% FBS and centrifuged at 300 g for 5 min. Diluted antibodies Fixable Viability Stain (APC-H7, BD Biosciences), CD45 (PerCP-Cy5.5, BD Biosciences), CD11B (FITC, BD Biosciences), F4/80 (BV421, BD Biosciences), CD206 (APC, BioLegend), and CD86 (PE-CY7, BD Biosciences) were shown to demonstrate macrophage polarization at 4°C dark for 30 min. Diluted antibodies Fixable Viability Stain (APC-H7, BD Biosciences), CD45 (PerCP-Cy5.5, BD Biosciences), CD11c (PE, BioLegend), I-A/I-E (FITC, BioLegend), CD80 (APC, BioLegend), and CD86 (PE-CY7, BD Biosciences) were used to demonstrate dendritic cell (DC) activation at 4°C dark for 30 min. The cells were washed twice with PBS solution containing 2% FBS and centrifuged at 300 g for 5 min. 200 µL of PBS containing 2% FBS was resuspended and later analyzed by flow cytometry (BD FACSVerse).

Single-cell and ST analyses were performed in R (V.4.2.2). To address compositional biases, raw cell-type counts underwent centered log-ratio (CLR) transformation. Dissimilarity was quantified using Aitchison distances. We then performed a paired permutational multivariate analysis of variance (PERMANOVA) via the adonis2 function, restricting permutations within patients (strata) to isolate treatment effects from interpatient heterogeneity. 58 The paired two-sided Wilcoxon test was used to evaluate cellular fraction differences between responders and non-responders before and after treatment. The unpaired two-sided t-test was used to compare signature scores of cell types and biological processes between R/NR groups and tumor/boundary regions. The permutation test was used to identify significant cell-type colocalization pairs. A two-way analysis of variance (ANOVA) test was used for apatinib at different times and concentrations. Apatinib in combination with chemotherapy was analyzed using a Student’s t-test. Tumor volume in mice was analyzed using a two-way ANOVA test. A Student’s t-test was used for other experiments in mice. The other statistical methods used are described in the captions. A two-sided p value <0.05 was considered statistically significant for all tests unless indicated otherwise (*p<0.05, **p<0.01, ***p<0.001).

sections.section: Transcriptomic Overview Of Neoadjuvant Chemoimmunotherapy In Escc
sections.text: To comprehensively characterize the dynamic evolution of the TME during NACI in ESCC, we collected paired tumor biopsies from nine treatment-naïve patients before therapy initiation (baseline) and after two cycles of NACI ( online supplemental table S1 ). Therapeutic responses were assessed according to the RECIST V.1.1 criteria. 59 Patients who achieved CR or PR were categorized as responders (R group), whereas those with SD were classified as non-responders (NR group). To dissect the cellular and spatial heterogeneity of the TME, all samples were subjected to droplet-based 5’ scRNA-seq and paired scTCR-seq. In parallel, ST profiling was performed on formalin-fixed paraffin-embedded (FFPE) surgical specimens from four patients: one treatment-naïve control (PRE) and three post-treatment cases representing different response categories (CR, PR and SD). Additionally, IHC and mIHC were carried out on a total of 14 paraffin-embedded samples ( online supplemental table S1 ). Finally, functional validation experiments were conducted to assess potential therapeutic targets in ESCC ( figure 1A ). Following stringent quality control, the scRNA-seq dataset encompassed 102,229 cells, with a median of 1,866 genes detected per cell, which were used for downstream analysis ( online supplemental figure S1A ). Integrated clustering across all samples identified nine major cell types, including epithelia, endothelia, fibroblast, NK-T, myeloid, neutrophil, mast, B and plasma cells, based on canonical marker gene expression profiles ( figure 1B ; online supplemental figure S1B,C ; online supplemental table S2 ). To account for the compositional nature of the data, we performed a CLR-based PERMANOVA, which confirmed no significant bias between treatment stages (p=0.328) or response groups (p=0.350) ( online supplemental figure S1D,E ). Notably, comparative analysis of cellular composition before and after treatment revealed an elevated proportion of ECs following therapeutic intervention ( figure 1C ; online supplemental figure S1F ). This finding was further supported by IHC results showing an elevated proportion of cells expressing VWF, a well-established EC marker, in post-treatment samples ( figure 1D,E ), reinforcing the notion of potential endothelial remodeling as a feature of NACI response. ST analysis provided deeper insights into the regional organization of the TME. H&E staining was first used to distinguish tumor and adjacent normal tissues in each sample ( figure 1F,G ). Following data quality filtering, tissue sections were segmented into distinct spatial domains based on gene expression profile ( online supplemental figure S2A–D ). Notably, marked regional reorganization was observed in both PR and CR cases following treatment. In non-responders, fibroblasts were predominantly localized within the tumor, whereas in responders, these cells tended to accumulate at the tumor periphery ( online supplemental figure S2E,F ). Given the established importance of the TME and its peripheral architecture in shaping therapeutic outcomes. 24 60 61 We applied spatially resolved cell-type specific scoring across transcriptomic spots to uncover structural reorganization within the tumor boundary. This approach uncovered a striking structural transformation—a dynamic 500 µm peritumorous transition zone specifically in responding tumors ( figure 1H ). We operationally define this region as the tumor boundary zone (TBZ), extending radially 500 µm from the invasive tumor front ( figure 1I ). Strikingly, responders exhibited significant spatial enrichment of ECs and fibroblasts within the TBZ microenvironment after treatment, suggesting a unique pattern of stromal reprogramming that may underlie effective immune activation and improved clinical outcomes ( figure 1J,K ; online supplemental figure S2G ). These findings highlight the importance of spatial context and stromal reorganization in NACI response, offering novel insights and potential strategies for improving clinical outcomes in patients with ESCC.

sections.section: Reprogramming Of Angiogenic To Antigen-Presenting Endothelial Cells
sections.text: To elucidate the relationship between EC heterogeneity and therapeutic response, we performed subclustering analysis and identified five distinct EC subpopulations based on expression of known marker genes ( figure 2A ; online supplemental figure S3A ; online supplemental table S3 ). Among those, ACKR1+ ECs specifically overexpressed chemokines associated with immune cell recruitment, including SELE and SELP , whereas RGCC+ ECs showed prominent enrichment of collagen-related genes such as COL4A1 and COL4A2 . Additionally, RGCC+ ECs shared features with PLVAP+ ECs, expressing markers like PLVAP and PLPP3 ( online supplemental figure S3B ). Previous studies have highlighted the role of ACKR1+ ECs in facilitating immune cell infiltration through chemokine presentation and cell adhesion. 62 In contrast, PLVAP+ ECs are known to be associated with M2-like macrophages and Tregs, thus contributing to the immunosuppressive TME. 63 GO enrichment analysis based on the cell-type specific markers further supported these functional distinctions: ACKR1+ ECs were enriched in antigen processing and presentation pathways, whereas RGCC+ ECs were predominantly involved in angiogenesis and extracellular matrix organization ( online supplemental figure S3C,D ). Importantly, therapeutic responders exhibited a significant post-treatment increase in the proportion of ACKR1+ ECs, accompanied by a decrease in RGCC+ ECs abundance. A clear inverse correlation was observed between the frequencies of these two EC subtypes, with the association becoming more pronounced after treatment ( figure 2B,C ; online supplemental figure S3E,F ). Comparative transcriptomic profiling revealed that ACKR1+ ECs expressed high levels of genes associated with antigen presentation and chemokine signaling ( HLA-DRA , HLA-DQA1 , SELE , SELP , IL33 ), whereas RGCC+ ECs exhibited elevated expression of collagen, angiogenesis and oncogenic genes ( COL4A1 , COL4A2 , FLT1 , KDR , CCND1 ). Functional enrichment analysis corroborated their distinct biological roles ( figure 2D,E ). These findings collectively suggest that distinct EC subpopulations may play critical yet differential roles in mediating responses to NACI. To explore the spatial context of these EC subpopulations, we applied cell-type specific signature activity scoring to ST data. This analysis revealed that ACKR1+ ECs were significantly enriched at the TBZ in responders compared with intratumoral regions ( figure 2F,G ). Notably, non-responders displayed minimal accumulation of ACKR1+ ECs at the tumor periphery ( figure 2H ). Correspondingly, antigen presentation pathways were strongly activated within the TBZ of responders ( figure 2F ; online supplemental figure S3G,H ). In contrast, RGCC+ ECs were predominantly located within the tumor lesions of non-responders ( figure 2F,I ), where they may contribute to a protumorigenic and immunosuppressive environment through collagen deposition and angiogenic signaling. Collectively, these findings suggest that NACI may exert its therapeutic effect, at least in part, by modulating the balance between immunostimulatory ACKR1+ ECs and immunosuppressive RGCC+ ECs. The enrichment of ACKR1+ ECs—particularly at the TBZ—may facilitate immune cell infiltration and enhance antitumor immunity through antigen presentation and chemokine secretion. Conversely, the persistence of RGCC+ ECs correlates with poor therapeutic response, likely due to their support of tumor-promoting stromal remodeling and immune exclusion.

sections.section: Divergent Roles Of Collagen And Inflammatory Cafs In Modulating Naci Efficacy
sections.text: CAFs are increasingly recognized as key regulators of tumor progression, metastasis and therapeutic resistance. 64 Emerging evidence highlights their functional heterogeneity and dynamic interactions with the TME, particularly in the context of immunotherapy. 65 With advances in single-cell sequencing technologies, the diversity and plasticity of CAF populations have become central to understanding their differential roles in shaping immune responses. 66 In this study, we performed subclustering analysis of fibroblast populations and identified 11 distinct clusters based on canonical marker gene expression ( figure 3A ; online supplemental figure S4A ; online supplemental table S3 ). Leveraging previously reported signatures of CAF subtypes, we classified these clusters into known functional categories: inflammatory CAFs (iCAFs) and myofibroblastic CAFs (mCAFs). 45 Notably, CFD+ CAFs and APOD+ CAF exhibit high enrichment scores for iCAF, suggesting their involvement in proinflammatory signaling ( figure 3B ). These subpopulations displayed elevated expression of cytokines and other inflammation-related genes including CCL11 , IL16 and CXCL16 ( figure 3C ), consistent with the established role of iCAFs in recruiting and activating immune cells, potentially facilitating tumor cell destruction. 67 68 In contrast, MMP11+ CAFs and SFRP4+ CAFs showed strong mCAF enrichment scores 69 ( figure 3B ; online supplemental figure S4B ), characterized by high expression of collagen-related genes such as COL1A1 , COL1A2 and COL6A3 ( figure 3C ). These features align with the immunosuppressive and matrix remodeling functions of mCAFs, which may hinder immune infiltration and contribute to therapy resistance. 67 Dynamic changes in CAF composition were observed following NACI. Specifically, the proportions of CFD+ CAF and APOD+ CAF significantly increased post-treatment, whereas those of MMP11+ CAF and MKI67+ CAF decreased ( figure 3D ; online supplemental figure S4C ). This shift was most pronounced in responders ( figure 3E ; online supplemental figure S4D ), indicating that NACI may favor the expansion of immunostimulatory CAF subsets. ST analysis further revealed the spatial localization patterns of these CAF subtypes. Both CFD+ CAF and APOD+ CAF—representing iCAFs—were prominently enriched in the TBZ compared with intratumoral regions following treatment. Notably, CFD+ CAFs maintained heightened enrichment in responders across both TBZ and tumor core in responders ( figure 3F–H ; online supplemental figure S4E,F ), suggesting their sustained presence in immune-reactive niches. Conversely, the mCAF-like subtypes SFRP4+ CAF and MMP11+ CAF were preferentially localized within tumor lesions of non-responders ( figure 3F,G,I ; online supplemental figure S4E,G ), where they likely contribute to the formation of a dense, immunosuppressive extracellular matrix barrier. These findings suggest that NACI may reshape the CAF landscape, promoting the accumulation of inflammation-associated CAFs within TBZ, thereby enhancing immune cell recruitment from the tumor periphery. In contrast, tumors from non-responders remain dominated by collagen-producing mCAFs, which may impede immune cell infiltration and limit therapeutic efficacy.

sections.section: Rgs1+ Cd8+ T Cells And Ctla4+ Tregs Are Associated With Naci Efficacy
sections.text: The functional diversity of T cell subsets plays a central role in determining the efficacy of cancer immunotherapy. 70 Accumulating evidence across multiple tumor types has identified CXCL13+CD8+ T cells as a promising biomarker for immunotherapy responses, often associated with effective antitumor immunity. 22 71 72 In this study, we aimed to characterize the dynamics and functional states of T cell populations during NACI in ESCC. IHC revealed a significant increase in the pan-T cell marker CD3+ in responders post-treatment compared with baseline levels ( online supplemental figure S5A,B ), suggesting enhanced immune activation in these patients. Using unsupervised clustering of scRNA-seq data, we identified 12 transcriptionally distinct CD8+ T cell clusters defined by unique marker gene combinations ( figure 4A ; online supplemental figure S5C ; online supplemental table S3 ). Among these, the RGS1+CD8+ T cell subset showed an increase in abundance after treatment in responders ( online supplemental figure S5D ), indicating its potential role in mediating therapeutic effects. To further dissect the clonal dynamics of T cell responses, we performed longitudinal scTCR-seq analysis across time points and patient groups stratified by treatment efficacy. Before treatment, no significant differences in T cell clonality were observed among patients with distinct treatment responses. After treatment, responders exhibited increased T cell clonality and a trend toward decreased T cell diversity ( online supplemental figure S5E,F ). Clonosize analysis of T cell subtypes with identical TCR sequences revealed treatment-associated expansion of both RGS1+CD8+ and CXCL13+CD8+ T cell clones in responders, contrasting with clonal contraction observed in non-responders ( figure 4B ). Subsequently, a comparative analysis was performed to quantify the proportion of TCRs exhibiting significant expansion (Ex) within different CD8+T cell subsets during treatment. It was found that the proportion of Ex TCRs in RGS1+CD8+ T cells increased markedly after treatment ( online supplemental figure S5G ). Moreover, the majority of Ex TCRs in responders were enriched in RGS1+CD8+ T cells, CXCL13+CD8+ T cells, CISH+CD8+ T cells and THBS1+CD8+ T cells, while FGFBP2+CD8+ T cells dominated among expanded clones in non-responders ( figure 4C,D ). These findings suggest that NACI preferentially promotes the clonal expansion of functionally active both RGS1+CD8+ and CXCL13+CD8+ T cell populations in responders, contributing to improved therapeutic outcomes To explore the molecular profiles associated with clonal expansion, we conducted differential gene expression analysis between significantly expanded (Ex) and non-naive non-significantly expanded (ex) CD8+ T cell subsets across treatment-response groups, both pretreatment and post-treatment. CD8+T cells from responders exhibited upregulation of genes linked to CXCL13+CD8+ and RGS1+CD8+ T cell subsets, including CXCL13 , KIR2DL4 , RGS1 , SPRY1 , MYO1E and LRRN3 . Notably, these genes remained largely unchanged in the Ex CD8+ T cell from non-responders ( online supplemental figure S5H ). Further dissection revealed that pretreatment Ex CD8+ T cells in responders expressed high levels of CXCL13+CD8+ T cell-associated genes, such as SNX9 , TIGIT , CXCL13 , ENTPD1 and TNFRSF18 . In contrast, post-treatment Ex CD8+ T cells in responders predominantly expressed RGS1+CD8+ T cell-associated genes, including PHLDA1 , RGS1 , RGS2 , SPRY1 , MYO1E and LRRN3 ( figure 4E ). These results support the hypotheses that CXCL13+CD8+ T cells may serve as a predictive biomarker for predicting therapeutic efficacy, while RGS1+CD8+ T cells emerge as key mediators of therapeutic response following NACI. Pseudotime analysis revealed a significant increase in clonosize over pseudotime, particularly within CXCL13+CD8+ T cells and RGS1+CD8+ T cells ( online supplemental figure S5I ). Notably, CXCL13+CD8+ T cells exhibited a stronger tendency toward exhaustion, whereas RGS1+CD8+ T cells were more inclined to a tissue-resident memory phenotype ( online supplemental figure S5J,K ). Tracking TCR clonotype sharing across clusters and timepoints provided further insight into lineage relationships between CD8+ T cell subsets. Strikingly, in responders, we observed substantial TCR overlap between pretreatment CXCL13+CD8+ T cell clonotypes and post-treatment RGS1+CD8+ T cells ( figure 4F ), suggesting a potential transitional or differentiation trajectory induced by NACI. This observation implies that NACI may drive the conversion of CXCL13+CD8+ T cells into RGS1+CD8+ T cells, thereby enhancing antitumor immunity. While this hypothesis requires further experimental validation, it opens new avenues for developing immunotherapeutic strategies that modulate T cell fate decisions. ST analysis corroborated these findings by revealing that both CXCL13+CD8+ T cells and RGS1+CD8+ T cells were significantly enriched in both tumor regions and TBZ of responders ( figure 4G,H ), underscoring their spatially coordinated infiltration and functional relevance in NACI response. In addition to CD8+ T cells, our analysis of CD4+ T cell populations highlighted a prominent presence of Tregs ( figure 4I ; online supplemental figure S6A ; online supplemental table S3 ). Previous studies have demonstrated that CTLA4 -expressing Tregs suppress antitumor immunity by inhibiting costimulatory signals via binding to B7 molecules on antigen-presenting cells. 73 Notably, TNFRSF4+ Tregs exhibited elevated expression of CTLA4 ( online supplemental figure S6A ), identifying them as a potentially immunosuppressive subset. Following treatment, responders demonstrated a marked reduction in the frequency of TNFRSF4+ Tregs ( figure 4J ; online supplemental figure S6B,C ), accompanied by a decrease in the proportion of expanded TNFRSF4+ Tregs clones ( figure 4K ). mIHC further confirmed that CTLA4+FOXP3+CD4+ T cells are associated with poor therapeutic outcomes ( figure 4L ; online supplemental figure S6D ), reinforcing the notion that depletion of immunosuppressive Tregs contributes to NACI efficacy. These findings suggest that the depletion of CTLA4+ Treg cells may play a role in the therapeutic efficacy of NACI. The combination of PD-1 monoclonal antibodies (mAbs) and anti-CTLA-4 mAbs may potentially represent a promising therapeutic strategy for ESCC. Given the relatively stable proportional abundance of major immune subsets and CD8+ T cell subsets post-treatment, we evaluated whether the therapy induced transcriptomic state transitions. Analysis of established immune effector and exhaustion gene signatures revealed complex, subset-specific functional reprogramming. For example, within the major immune subsets, NK/T cells exhibited an overall decrease in exhaustion and regulatory signatures post-treatment, along with trends toward increased chemokine-related and Th17-related signals ( online supplemental figure S7A,B ). While certain subsets (such as CXCL13+CD8+ T cells and TNFRSF4+Tregs) exhibited an attenuation of exhaustion-related programs, other subsets displayed distinct, heterogeneous alterations across chemotactic, TCR signaling, and helper-like functional modules ( online supplemental figure S7C–F ). These multidirectional transcriptomic shifts suggest that the cellular components undergo significant functional plasticity, even when their overall numbers remain stable.

sections.section: Apoe+ Macrophage Depletion And Cd1C+ Cdc2 Expansion
sections.text: The myeloid compartment plays a pivotal role in shaping the tumor immune microenvironment and modulating responses to immunotherapy. Among myeloid cells, macrophages and DCs are particularly influential: M1-like macrophages typically exhibit proinflammatory and antitumor properties by promoting T cell activation and cytokine production, whereas M2-like macrophages contribute to immune suppression and tumor progression by fostering an immunotolerant environment. 74 DCs, on the other hand, serve as central orchestrators of adaptive immunity through antigen presentation, costimulation and T cell priming. As such, targeting DC function and reprogramming macrophage polarization have emerged as promising strategies in cancer immunotherapy. 75 Single-cell profiling delineated the myeloid compartment into 11 transcriptionally distinct subpopulations, encompassing macrophage subsets, DC lineages and monocytic clusters ( online supplemental figure S8A,B ; online supplemental table S3 ). Among these, CD1C+ cDC2s exhibited strong expression of genes related to antigen presentation, such as CD1C, CD1E, HLA-DRB5 . In contrast, APOE+ macrophages displayed a gene expression signature characteristic of M2 polarization, with elevated levels of APOE, APOC1, CCL18, and showed high scores in M2 macrophage-specific gene modules ( online supplemental figure S8B,C ). 47 Notably, following NACI, we observed a marked reduction in the proportion of APOE+ macrophages, suggesting a depletion of immunosuppressive myeloid cells within the TME. Concomitantly, there was an obvious increase in the frequency of CD1C+ cDC2s ( online supplemental figure S8D ), indicating a shift toward a more immunostimulatory myeloid composition. This dynamic change was especially pronounced among patients who responded favorably to treatment ( online supplemental figure S8E ), further supporting the notion that myeloid reprogramming contributes to improved therapeutic outcomes. ST analysis added spatial context to these findings, revealing a positive correlation between CD1C+ cDC2 abundance within the tumor region and therapeutic efficacy ( online supplemental figure S8F,G ). Taken together, these results demonstrate that NACI induces profound remodeling of the myeloid compartment in ESCC, characterized by a reduction in immunosuppressive APOE+ macrophages and a concomitant expansion of antigen-presenting cDC2s. This shift reflects a broader transition from an immunologically “cold” TME to a more inflamed and permissive state, which appears to be closely linked with treatment response.

sections.section: Vegfa–Vegfr2 Axis Activation In Non-Responder Tumor Microenvironments
sections.text: Tumor-intrinsic features play a critical role in shaping disease progression and resistance to therapy, particularly in the context of NACI. To better understand the molecular and cellular mechanisms underlying treatment resistance in ESCC, we performed detailed cluster analysis on the epithelial cells followed by inferCNV-based classification to distinguish normal epithelial cells from malignant counterparts 40 ( figure 5A ; online supplemental figure S9A–C ). Post-therapeutic evaluation revealed a substantial depletion in the overall proportion of malignant cells, consistent with therapeutic impact in responsive tumors ( figure 5B ). Non-responder patients displayed significantly higher CNV burdens compared with responders, suggesting that the higher CNV burden may contribute to therapeutic evasion ( figure 5C ). Notably, malignant cells exhibited substantial interpatient heterogeneity in gene expression profiles, underscoring the complexity of tumor adaptation under immune pressure ( figure 5D ; online supplemental figure S9D ). To identify potential drivers of resistance, we conducted the differential expression analyses comparing samples between non-responders and responders pretreatment and post-treatment. Compared with responders, functional enrichment analysis of genes upregulated in non-responders both pretreatment and post-treatment revealed significant enrichment in pathways related to cell–cell adhesion, hypoxia, angiogenesis, and VEGF signaling ( figure 5E ; online supplemental figure S9E,F ), highlighting a coordinated transcriptional program associated with an immunosuppressive and therapy-resistant TME. Among these, the VEGFA signaling axis emerged as a particularly compelling candidate. Compared with responders, VEGFA was persistently overexpressed in non-responders across both pretreatment and post-treatment phases ( figure 5F ), indicating its potential role in mediating adaptive resistance to NACI. Single-cell profiling further identified a subpopulation of ECs expressing RGCC (RGCC+ ECs, figure 2E ) with elevated levels of VEGFR2 , the primary receptor for VEGFA . Intriguingly, this RGCC+ ECs was inversely correlated with treatment response, suggesting a functional link between VEGF signaling and NACI failure. The mIHC results corroborate these findings, revealing a significant increase in the frequencies of VEGFA+ and VEGFR2+ cells in post-treatment tissues from non-responders compared with responders ( figure 5G,H ). These observations prompted us to explore the spatial organization of VEGFA and VEGFR2 expression using ST data. Employing a GMM, we classified spatial spots into four categories based on expression patterns: VEGFA-only, VEGFR2-only, coexpressing (VEGFA–VEGFR2) and other (neither expressed). Given the paracrine nature of VEGF signaling, which typically operates within an effective range of up to 200 µm, we applied repeated random sampling to quantify the proximity of VEGFA and VEGFR2 coexpression within defined spatial radii. Strikingly, non-responder tumors exhibited significantly increased spatial coexpression of VEGFA and VEGFR2 at both 100 µm and 200 µm distances ( figure 5I,J ). These data collectively implicate angiogenesis-related VEGFA–VEGFR2 signaling activation within the TME as a potential mediator of NACI resistance in ESCC.

sections.section: Vegf Modulates Therapeutic Efficacy Via Collagen-Remodeling Stromal Cells
sections.text: Our study revealed distinct cellular ecosystems associated with NACI outcomes in ESCC, highlighting the central role of VEGF signaling in shaping an immunosuppressive TME. In non-responder tumors, we observed enrichment of several key stromal and immune components within the tumor regions, including RGCC+ ECs, MMP11+ CAFs, TNFRSF4+ Tregs and APOE+ macrophages. To better understand how these populations interact and contribute to therapeutic resistance, we performed cell–cell interaction analyses to further investigate the potential mechanism/interplay underlying their associations. Non-responders showed elevated baseline activation of the VEGF signaling compared with responders prior to treatment ( online supplemental figure S10A,B ). Specifically, malignant epithelial cells in these patients exhibited elevated expression of VEGFA/B , meanwhile RGCC1+ ECs displayed higher expression levels of VEGFR1/2 ( online supplemental figure S11A ). Further analysis identified significantly enriched ligand–receptor interactions between malignant epithelial cells and RGCC+ ECs mediated by the VEGF axis in non-responders ( figure 6A ), suggesting that tumor-derived VEGF may directly promote the expansion or activation of this specific endothelial subpopulation. This interaction may thereby contribute to the establishment of a vascular niche that limits immune infiltration and dampens therapeutic efficacy. In addition to their angiogenic properties, RGCC+ ECs were found to express high levels of collagen-associated genes such as COL4A1 and COL4A2 ( online supplemental figure S11B ). Intriguingly, our analysis revealed that these RGCC+ ECs may engage in extensive crosstalk with multiple other cell types—including malignant epithelial cells, TNFRSF4+ Tregs, MMP11+ CAFs, and APOE+ macrophages—via collagen-associated receptor-ligand pairs involving ITGB1 , SDC1 and SDC4 ( figure 6A,B ). These receptors have been previously implicated in tumor progression, immune evasion, and resistance to therapy, 76 78 further supporting the idea that RGCC+ ECs may contribute to an immunosuppressive milieu through extracellular matrix remodeling and cell adhesion signaling. Consistently, MMP11+ CAFs showed robust expression of collagen-related genes such as COL1A1 , COL1A2 , COL6A1 , COL6A2 and COL6A3 ( online supplemental figure S11B ), reinforcing the notion that collagen remodeling plays a central role in the formation of a fibrotic, immune-excluded TME. Cell–cell interaction analysis confirmed enhanced engagement of these MMP11+ CAFs with malignant epithelial cells, RGCC+ECs, TNFRSF4+ Tregs and APOE+ macrophages via the collagen-associated ligand–receptor pairs in non-responders prior to treatment ( online supplemental figure S11C ). These data suggest that a collagen-rich, structurally reinforced tumor stroma is already established before therapy initiation in non-responsive patients, potentially limiting immune cell access and impairing the efficacy of immunotherapeutic interventions—a phenomenon consistent with previous reports in solid tumors. 26 ST profiling further validated this hypothesis, showing that genes associated with both angiogenesis and collagen deposition were enriched within tumor regions of non-responders ( figure 6D,E ). To explore the spatial proximity of cell types with potential interactions, we integrated single-cell transcriptomic and ST data to assign individual cells to their corresponding spatial coordinates 53 ( online supplemental figure S11F ). Our analysis revealed that RGCC+ ECs colocalized closely with MMP11+ CAFs and TNFRSF4+ Tregs within the tumor regions of non-responders, forming a tightly associated immunosuppressive niche—an interaction pattern notably absent or much less pronounced in responders ( figure 6F,H ). In contrast, post-treatment samples from responders revealed a markedly different cellular landscape, characterized by the emergence of antigen-presenting stromal elements and enhanced immune coordination. Specifically, CFD+ CAFs, APOD+ CAFs and ACKR1+ ECs formed extensive interactions with CD8+ T cells via MHC-I molecules, including HLA-A , HLA-B , HLA-C and HLA-E ( figure 6C ). Spatial analysis demonstrated that these cell clusters, along with MHC-I-associated gene signatures and the gene set exhibiting marked TCR clonal expansion in CD8+ T cells from post-treatment responders, were highly enriched within the TBZ area ( online supplemental figure S11D,E ). Within this spatial region, ACKR1+ ECs and CFD+ CAFs exhibited strong spatial colocalization with CD8+ T cells, a relationship that was more pronounced than that observed between RGCC+ ECs and MMP11+ CAFs ( figure 6G,H ; online supplemental figure S11G–I ), underscoring the functional relevance of these stromal subsets in promoting effective antitumor immunity. Taken together, these findings reveal a potential critical mechanism by which VEGF shapes the tumor microenvironment to favor immunosuppressive and therapeutic resistance in ESCC. Specifically, VEGF-enriched niches in non-responders drive the accumulation and functional specialization of collagen-remodeling stromal cells—particularly RGCC+ ECs and MMP11+ CAFs—that collectively form a physical and biochemical barrier to immune infiltration. Consistently, collagen fibers were more abundant in the tumors of non-responders ( online supplemental figure S12A ). Conversely, in responders, the TBZ becomes enriched with antigen-presenting stromal cells—such as ACKR1+ ECs and CFD+ CAFs—that facilitate the spatial integration and functional activation of CD8+ T cells, thereby promoting a more favorable immune response and improved clinical outcomes.

sections.section: Strategies Targeting Vegfr2 To Increase Therapeutic Efficacy
sections.text: Given the evidence implicating VEGF signaling in NACI resistance, as demonstrated throughout this study, we sought to investigate whether targeting its key receptor, VEGFR2, could enhance therapeutic efficacy in ESCC. To evaluate this hypothesis, we employed VEGFR2 mAbs in murine tumor models and assessed their impact when combined with PD-1 blockade—a standard immunotherapeutic approach. Our results show that anti-VEGFR2 mAb significantly enhances the antitumor efficacy of PD-1 inhibition in a murine esophageal cancer model ( figure 7A–C ). Importantly, this combination therapy was well tolerated, with no obvious adverse impact on body weight or hepatic and renal function parameters in mice ( online supplemental figure S12B,C ). Histopathological evaluation via H&E staining further confirmed the absence of major organ toxicity following combination therapy ( online supplemental figure S12D ). Beyond its established role in angiogenesis, our mechanistic analysis revealed that VEGFR2 blockade profoundly reshapes the tumor immune microenvironment. Flow cytometry analysis revealed a marked increase in both the frequency of activated DC cells, as well as a shift toward a more proinflammatory M1-like macrophage phenotype ( figure 7D,E ). These immunomodulatory effects were accompanied by enhanced infiltration of CD8+ T cells into the tumor parenchyma, as evidenced by IHC analysis, which also revealed increased numbers of granzyme B-positive cells and apoptotic cells within the tumor tissue ( figure 7F,G ). Overall, these findings suggest that combining anti-VEGFR2 mAb with immunotherapy may synergistically enhance the activation of antitumor immune cells, thereby promoting tumor cell apoptosis. The clinical relevance of VEGFR2-targeted therapy has been previously established in various malignancies, where such agents are often used in later lines of treatment. 79 However, our study extends these observations by demonstrating that VEGFR2 inhibition can also enhance the efficacy of conventional chemotherapy in ESCC. We evaluated Apatinib, a small-molecule tyrosine kinase inhibitor selective for VEGFR2, and found that it exhibited notable intrinsic antitumor activity against ESCC cell lines ( figure 7H ). 80 81 More importantly, when apatinib was combined with standard-of-care chemotherapeutic agents—including albumin-bound paclitaxel and cisplatin—it significantly enhanced tumor cell growth inhibition in vitro ( figure 7I,J ; online supplemental figure S12E,F ). These synergistic effects suggest that incorporating VEGFR2 inhibitors into neoadjuvant or concurrent treatment regimens may offer substantial benefits in patients with ESCC, particularly those at risk of developing resistance to NACI alone. These findings collectively support the integration of VEGFR2-targeted strategies into multimodal therapeutic approaches for ESCC. By simultaneously inhibiting angiogenic signals and enhancing immune activation, VEGFR2 blockade appears to overcome key barriers to effective antitumor immunity. This dual mechanism not only disrupts the structural and metabolic support of the tumor but also reprograms the immune landscape to favor immune cell infiltration and function. As such, combining VEGFR2 inhibitors with immune checkpoint blockade or chemotherapy represents a promising avenue for improving clinical outcomes in ESCC and warrants further investigation in clinical trials.

Despite the growing promise of NACI in locally advanced ESCC, significant heterogeneity in clinical response remains a major barrier to its broader success. This variability reflects the complex and dynamic nature of the TME, which plays a central role in determining therapeutic outcomes. To elucidate the underlying mechanisms driving this heterogeneity and identify potential actionable therapeutic strategies, we conducted an in-depth analysis of the TME in a cohort of patients with ESCC who underwent NACI. Leveraging scRNA-seq/scTCR-seq combined with spatial transcriptome profiling, we generated a comprehensive map of cellular composition, functional states, and spatial organization within the TME before and after treatment. These data enabled us to delineate key molecular and cellular determinants of response and resistance, offering new insights into how NACI interacts with the tumor ecosystem in ESCC. Based on established literature, neoadjuvant chemotherapy remodels the ESCC tumor microenvironment primarily through immunogenic cell death and immune cell reorganization. Notably, chemoimmunotherapy further amplifies antitumor immunity beyond chemotherapy by boosting T-cell proliferation, reinvigorating Texs, expanding a proliferative exhausted CD8+ subset, and increasing DC activity. In this context, our integrative spatial and single-cell transcriptomic analysis reveals that these combined mechanisms give rise to unique immune and stromal landscapes linked to differential therapeutic responses. 82 84 In responders, we observed a marked reduction in VEGF signaling activity alongside a shift toward a more permissive immune environment. Notably, the TBZ was enriched with ACKR1+ ECs, CFD+ CAFs and RGS1+CD8+ T cells—cellular subsets that appeared to coordinate a localized immune response. Immunotherapy has been shown to exert divergent effects on Tex populations across different cancers. 85 For instance, in basal cell carcinoma, squamous cell carcinoma and breast cancer, immunotherapy expands terminal Tex cells. Conversely, in lung cancer and melanoma, it enriches precursor exhausted T (Texp) cells. 3886 88 This disparity may stem from varying degrees of immune suppression within distinct tumor types. Previous studies have shown that ESCC presents an immunologically “cold” microenvironment dominated by Tregs and terminal Tex cells. 89 Our findings suggest a unique pattern in ESCC. Specifically, we observed expansion of RGS1+CD8+ T cells and CXCL13+CD8+ T cells, both of which exhibit features of terminal exhaustion, including overexpression of multiple immune checkpoint molecules. Intriguingly, TCR repertoire analysis revealed clonal overlap between post-treatment RGS1+CD8+ T cells and pretreatment CXCL13+CD8+ T cells, indicating a potential transformation from CXCL13+ Tex cells to RGS1+CD8+ T cells following therapy. However, unlike Texp, which are typically associated with better therapeutic responsiveness, RGS1+CD8+ T cells lacked canonical Texp markers, suggesting that their functional state may represent a distinct transitional phase. The absence of clear Texp clusters in our dataset highlights the profound immunosuppressive nature of the ESCC microenvironment and underscores the need for larger-scale studies or in-depth experiment validation to fully characterize T cell plasticity in this disease. Beyond immune reprogramming, our data also highlight a coordinated remodeling of the stromal compartment in responders. The TBZ was notably enriched with ACKR1+ ECs and CFD+ CAFs, both of which exhibited gene expression profiles consistent with immune-supportive functions. These stromal subsets were not only transcriptionally active but also spatially proximal to infiltrating CD8+ T cells, suggesting a direct role in facilitating immune engagement. Mechanistically, we found evidence of MHC-I-mediated interactions between these stromal cells and CD8+ T cells, pointing to a previously underappreciated non-canonical antigen-presenting axis that may enhance local immune activation. Importantly, similar stromal cells have been reported in patients with colorectal cancer responding to immunotherapy. 90 Our findings thus propose that modulating stromal-immune crosstalk through MHC-I pathways could be a promising strategy to improve NACI efficacy in ESCC and other solid tumors with organized stromal-immune architectures. In contrast, non-responders exhibited a markedly different tumor ecosystem characterized by a dominant angiogenesis program driven by VEGF signaling.
